The disclaimer refers to muscle-invasive bladder cancer, although the guideline addresses testosterone deficiency.
Some words and passages contain apparent text-recognition artifacts.
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses how clinicians diagnose testosterone deficiency, assess its possible causes, and counsel men about treatment benefits and uncertainties. It covers testosterone therapy, fertility-preserving alternatives, safety considerations, and follow-up, including care for men with cardiovascular disease or a history of prostate cancer.

care_settings: Research settings for locally advanced or metastatic prostate cancer
target_population: Men with suspected or diagnosed testosterone deficiency
Men with testosterone deficiency who wish to preserve fertility
Men with testosterone deficiency who have or are at risk for cardiovascular disease
Men with testosterone deficiency and a history of prostate cancer

conditions.name: testosterone deficiency
conditions.description: Clinical diagnosis requires low total testosterone together with relevant symptoms and/or signs. The guideline uses total testosterone below 300 ng/dL to support the diagnosis and requires confirmation on separate early-morning measurements.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Reported symptoms may include reduced energy or endurance, poorer work or physical performance, fatigue, bitemporal hemianopsia, anosmia, depression, reduced motivation or concentration, impaired memory, irritability, infertility, reduced sex drive, and changes in erectile function. Relevant examination findings may involve body habitus, virilization, gynecomastia, or testicular abnormalities.

subtypes.name: hypergonadatropic hypogonadism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Elevated follicle-stimulating hormone in a patient with testosterone deficiency typically indicates impaired spermatogenesis.

subtypes.name: testosterone deficient patients with low or low/normal LH levels
subtypes.distinguishing_features: This LH pattern prompts prolactin testing and may affect the choice of additional investigations and fertility-preserving treatment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support and confirm a diagnosis of low testosterone.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Obtain two measurements on separate occasions, both in the early morning, preferably using the same laboratory and measurement method. Consider testing even without associated symptoms or signs in patients with unexplained anemia, bone density loss, diabetes, chemotherapy exposure, testicular radiation exposure, HIV/AIDS, chronic narcotic use, male infertility, pituitary dysfunction, or chronic corticosteroid use.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A level below 300 ng/dL supports the diagnosis; the guideline describes consistently <300 ng/dL on at least two measurements as its threshold. Symptoms and/or signs are also required for a clinical diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify signs associated with low testosterone.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Assess body habitus, body hair in androgen-dependent areas, body mass index or waist circumference, gynecomastia, testicular presence, size, consistency and masses, varicocele, and prostate size and morphology.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help establish the cause of testosterone deficiency and guide additional testing.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Low or low/normal LH together with low testosterone prompts prolactin measurement; total testosterone <150 ng/dL with this LH pattern warrants pituitary MRI regardless of prolactin.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When low testosterone is accompanied by low or low/normal LH.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Repeat an elevated result to assess whether the initial finding was spurious. Persistent elevation can indicate a pituitary tumor, such as a prolactinoma, and warrants endocrine evaluation if its cause is unknown.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When total testosterone is <150 ng/dL and LH is low or low/normal, regardless of prolactin level.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess breast symptoms or gynecomastia before testosterone therapy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In testosterone deficient patients presenting with breast symptoms or gynecomastia.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An elevated baseline level warrants referral to an endocrinologist.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before treatment in men wishing to preserve current fertility.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Evaluate testicular size, consistency, and descent.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before treatment in men wishing to preserve current fertility.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Elevation in the setting of testosterone deficiency is typically indicative of impaired spermatogenesis.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider when follicle-stimulating hormone is elevated in the setting of testosterone deficiency.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A sperm concentration <5 million sperm per mL constitutes severe oligospermia in the guideline.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Offer to patients with severe oligospermia (sperm concentration <5 million sperm per mL) or non-obstructive azoospermia.
Offer to patients with severe oligospermia (sperm concentration <5 million sperm per mL) or non-obstructive azoospermia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish a baseline before testosterone therapy and monitor for polycythemia.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before initiating testosterone therapy and during treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: If baseline Hct exceeds 50%, consider withholding therapy until its cause has been investigated. An on-treatment Hct 54% warrants intervention.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help exclude prostate cancer before testosterone therapy and monitor prostate cancer where applicable.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before treatment in men over 40 years of age; repeat an elevated baseline result. Monitor patients with prostate cancer receiving testosterone therapy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: If two baseline PSA results raise suspicion for prostate cancer, consider further evaluation before treatment.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider before testosterone therapy when two baseline PSA results raise suspicion for prostate cancer.
Consider before testosterone therapy when two baseline PSA results raise suspicion for prostate cancer.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: Offered as part of reproductive genetics testing for severe oligospermia (sperm concentration <5 million sperm per mL) or non-obstructive azoospermia.
Offered as part of reproductive genetics testing for severe oligospermia (sperm concentration <5 million sperm per mL) or non-obstructive azoospermia.

follow_up.schedule: Check total testosterone after treatment begins at an interval appropriate to the formulation: between two to four weeks for topical gels, patches, and intranasal formulations, with therapy applied on the testing day; no earlier than four weeks for anastrozole, clomiphene citrate, or hCG; no earlier than three to four cycles for shortacting intramuscular or subcutaneous testosterone cypionate or enanthate; and halfway between the first two 10-week injections for intramuscular testosterone undecanoate. For long-acting subcutaneous pellets, measure testosterone two to four weeks after the initial implant and again after 10-12 weeks. Once therapeutic levels are attained, check serum testosterone every 6-12 months. Discuss stopping therapy three to six months after initiation if testosterone normalizes without improvement in symptoms or signs.
recommended_tests: Serum total testosterone to assess attainment and maintenance of the target level and guide dose or administration-frequency adjustments.
Hemoglobin and hematocrit during testosterone therapy to detect polycythemia.
PSA in patients with prostate cancer receiving testosterone therapy, on the same schedule used for men without testosterone deficiency; clinicians may test more frequently.
long_term_effects: Discuss the uncertain long-term recovery of spermatogenesis after exogenous testosterone with patients interested in future fertility. In contraceptive studies, two-thirds of males recovered sperm in the ejaculate within six months after cessation, whereas 10% did not do so until the second year; recovery in infertile males is not well-established.
An on-treatment Hct 54% warrants intervention, such as reducing the dose or temporarily discontinuing therapy.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The treatment target is a total testosterone level in the normal physiologic range of 450-600 ng/dL together with improvement in symptoms or signs. If target levels are achieved without symptomatic improvement, reassess whether testosterone deficiency explains the symptoms; the guideline states that continuing treatment in this circumstance has no utility. Patients receiving testosterone therapy should report possible cardiovascular symptoms at routine follow-up. Evaluate PSA recurrence in patients with prostate cancer as it would be evaluated in untreated men.

recognition: Measure hemoglobin and Hct before treatment and monitor Hct during treatment.
Trials associated injectable testosterone with the largest treatment-related increases in hemoglobin/Hct; the guideline could not establish comparative polycythemia incidence across formulations.

management.actions: Consider deferring testosterone therapy until the cause has been formally investigated.
Intervene, for example by reducing the dose or temporarily stopping treatment.

prevention: Obtain baseline hemoglobin and Hct and explain the increased polycythemia risk before offering testosterone therapy.
toxicities.dose_modifications: An on-treatment Hct 54% warrants intervention, which may include dose reduction or temporary discontinuation.

toxicities.event: Impaired spermatogenesis, severe oligospermia, or azoospermia
recognition: Exogenous testosterone can disrupt spermatogenesis and leave men severely oligospermic or azoospermic.
Recovery of sperm in the ejaculate after treatment cessation varies considerably.

management.severity: Future reproductive plans while receiving exogenous testosterone
management.actions: Stop testosterone before beginning attempts to conceive. Discuss the variable timing and extent of spermatogenesis recovery; recovery after discontinuation is not well established in infertile men.

prevention: Do not prescribe exogenous testosterone therapy to men currently trying to conceive.
Before treatment, discuss the possible long-term effects on spermatogenesis with patients interested in future fertility.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Exogenous testosterone should be stopped in advance of attempts to conceive.

toxicities.event: Gynecomastia or other breast symptoms during treatment
recognition: Breast pain, breast tenderness, nipple tenderness, or gynecomastia may occur during treatment, although symptomatic breast effects are uncommon.
Estradiol may rise as total testosterone rises during treatment.

management.severity: Gynecomastia or breast symptoms developing during treatment
management.actions: Consider a period of observation guided by clinical judgment, because symptoms sometimes subside.
Refer the patient to an endocrinologist.

prevention: Measure serum estradiol before starting testosterone therapy in testosterone deficient patients with breast symptoms or gynecomastia.

toxicities.event: Transference of topical testosterone and adverse effects in exposed people
recognition: Women and children are at greatest risk of effects that include virilization, precocious puberty, and hyperandrogenism.
Observe children for signs or symptoms of early puberty.
prevention: Discuss transference risk with patients using testosterone gels/creams.
Avoid contact with application sites that have not been washed or covered.

recognition: Reported hepatic effects include abnormal liver function tests, cholestasis, and jaundice.
prevention: Do not prescribe alkylated oral testosterone; the guideline considers use of 17-alpha-akylated androgens inappropriate given the availability of other approved therapies.

toxicities.event: Possible cardiovascular events during testosterone therapy
recognition: Possible cardiovascular symptoms to report during follow-up include chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, and transient loss of consciousness.

The guideline states that evidence does not definitively establish whether testosterone therapy increases or decreases the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiovascular-related death, or allcause mortality.

management.actions: Do not start testosterone therapy for three to six months after the event. After that waiting period, the Panel considers treatment with close dosing and safety monitoring a possible option.

prevention: Before treatment, explain the uncertainty about cardiovascular benefit or harm.
Assess testosterone deficient patients for fixed and modifiable ASCVD risk factors.
Advise patients receiving testosterone therapy to report possible cardiovascular symptoms at routine follow-up.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Do not commence testosterone therapy for three to six months in patients with a history of cardiovascular events.

toxicities.event: Prostate-related events and uncertain prostate cancer risk
toxicities.incidence: In a meta-analysis by Calof et al. (2005) pooling 19 RCTs, allcause prostate-related events were significantly more frequent in the exogenous testosterone arm than in the placebo arm (OR¼1.79; CI: 1.07, 2.95), although events could have been counted more than once for an individual. Analyses of individual events found no statistically significant between-group difference for prostate cancer (OR¼1.09), PSA elevation to >4 ng/mL or PSA increase >1.5 ng/mL during treatment (OR¼1.19), any increase in International Prostate Symptom Score (OR¼1.08), or acute urinary retention (OR¼0.99).
recognition: The guideline reports no established link between testosterone therapy and the development of prostate cancer, while noting that the FDA retains a warning about potential risk.
An increase in PSA has been observed among treated men in high-risk groups after radical prostatectomy.

management.actions: Repeat PSA to check whether the elevation was spurious. If two baseline results suggest prostate cancer, consider more formal assessment, potentially including reflex testing (e.g., 4K or phi) and prostate biopsy with/without MRI, before treatment.

management.severity: PSA recurrence during testosterone therapy in a patient with prostate cancer
management.actions: Evaluate recurrence as in men who are not receiving testosterone therapy. Discussion of stopping treatment should include the possibility that PSA may decline.

prevention: Measure PSA before starting testosterone therapy in men over 40 years of age to reduce the risk of treating occult prostate cancer.
Monitor PSA in patients with prostate cancer receiving testosterone therapy on the same schedule used for men without testosterone deficiency; clinicians may test more frequently.

recognition: The guideline describes conflicting findings on a possible association with testosterone therapy and states that definitive evidence of a higher incidence is lacking.
Observational studies conducted after the FDA warning in June 2014 did not show an association between testosterone therapy and increased VTE risk.
prevention: Inform patients that a definitive link between testosterone therapy and a higher incidence of venous thromboembolic events has not been established.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Obtain hemoglobin and Hct before testosterone therapy and counsel patients about polycythemia risk; consider withholding treatment if baseline Hct exceeds 50% until its cause has been investigated.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients being considered for testosterone therapy

prophylaxis.recommendation: Measure PSA before starting testosterone therapy to reduce the risk of treating occult prostate cancer.
Do not prescribe exogenous testosterone therapy while a man is trying to conceive, and discuss its possible long-term effect on spermatogenesis with those planning future fertility.
prophylaxis.target_population: Men currently trying to conceive or interested in future fertility

prophylaxis.recommendation: Discuss transference risk, avoid contact with unwashed or uncovered application sites, and watch for signs or symptoms of early puberty in children.
prophylaxis.target_population: Users of topical testosterone preparations and people who may contact them, particularly women and children

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not prescribe alkylated oral testosterone because of its hepatic toxicity and the availability of other approved therapies.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients being considered for testosterone therapy

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not commence testosterone therapy following a cardiovascular event during the specified waiting period.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with a history of cardiovascular events

therapies_index.name: testosterone therapy
therapies_index.administration: The guideline advises using the lowest dose needed to reach a total testosterone level of 450-600 ng/dL, while assessing whether symptoms or signs improve.
key_toxicities: Exogenous testosterone can suppress spermatogenesis and may lead to severe oligospermia or azoospermia.
Gynecomastia or other breast symptoms can develop during treatment, although symptomatic cases are uncommon.
monitoring: Measure hemoglobin and hematocrit before treatment; consider withholding therapy if baseline Hct exceeds 50% until its cause is investigated. An on-treatment Hct of 54% warrants intervention, such as dose reduction or temporary discontinuation.
Check total testosterone after an interval appropriate to the formulation and then every 6-12 months once therapeutic levels have been reached.
Assess improvement in symptoms or signs. Discuss stopping treatment three to six months after initiation if testosterone normalizes without clinical improvement.

Measure PSA before treatment in men over 40 years of age. For patients with prostate cancer receiving testosterone, monitor PSA on the schedule used for men without testosterone deficiency; testing may be more frequent.
Ask patients to report possible cardiovascular symptoms, including chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness or transient loss of consciousness, at follow-up visits.

therapies_index.name: testosterone gels/creams
therapies_index.administration: Topical application; the preparation should be applied on the day of testosterone testing.
key_toxicities: Transfer to another person is possible. Women and children are at greatest risk of effects such as virilization, precocious puberty and hyperandrogenism.
monitoring: Check testosterone between two to four weeks after starting treatment.
Discuss transfer risk and watch for signs or symptoms of early puberty in children who may have been exposed.
Avoid others contacting application sites that have not been washed or covered.

therapies_index.name: testosterone patches
therapies_index.administration: The patch should be applied on the day testosterone is measured.
monitoring: Check testosterone between two to four weeks after starting treatment.

therapies_index.name: intranasal formulations
therapies_index.administration: Intranasal; the formulation should be administered on the day testosterone is measured.
monitoring: Check testosterone between two to four weeks after starting treatment.

therapies_index.name: testosterone cypionate
key_toxicities: Trials associated injectable testosterone with the greatest treatment-related increases in hemoglobin/Hct among the modalities discussed.
monitoring: Measure testosterone no earlier than three to four cycles after treatment begins.

therapies_index.name: enanthate
therapies_index.administration: Listed with testosterone cypionate as short-acting intramuscular or subcutaneous testosterone.
key_toxicities: Trials associated injectable testosterone with the greatest treatment-related increases in hemoglobin/Hct among the modalities discussed.
monitoring: Measure testosterone no earlier than three to four cycles after treatment begins.

therapies_index.name: testosterone undecanoate
therapies_index.administration: Long-acting intramuscular testosterone; the guideline refers to the first two 10-week injections.
key_toxicities: Trials associated injectable testosterone with the greatest treatment-related increases in hemoglobin/Hct among the modalities discussed.
monitoring: Obtain blood work halfway between the first two 10-week injections.

therapies_index.name: long-acting subcutaneous pellets
monitoring: Measure testosterone two to four weeks after the first implantation to assess whether the pellet number needs adjustment.
Repeat testosterone testing after 10-12 weeks to help determine when to administer the next implant.

therapies_index.name: alkylated oral testosterone
therapies_index.administration: Oral. The guideline advises clinicians not to prescribe it.
key_toxicities: The guideline associates Methyl testosterone with liver toxicity.

therapies_index.name: Methyl testosterone
approved_indications: Approved in the United States for treatment of testosterone deficiency.
therapies_index.administration: The guideline discusses it under alkylated oral testosterone, which it advises clinicians not to prescribe.
key_toxicities: Liver toxicity, including abnormal liver function tests, cholestasis and jaundice.

therapies_index.name: compounded testosterone
therapies_index.administration: Gels and creams are described as its most common forms. The guideline prefers commercially manufactured testosterone products when possible.
monitoring: Consider additional testosterone monitoring and dose adjustment because potency and quality can vary, including between samples from one pharmacy.

therapies_index.name: commercially manufactured testosterone products
therapies_index.administration: The guideline prefers these products to compounded testosterone when possible.

therapies_index.name: aromatase inhibitors
therapies_index.mechanism: Described among alternative agents that increase the body's own testosterone production; the guideline does not specify a distinct mechanism for this class.
therapies_index.administration: May be used alone or with the other listed alternative agents in men with testosterone deficiency who want to maintain fertility.

therapies_index.name: human chorionic gonadotropin
therapies_index.mechanism: Described as promoting endogenous testosterone production.
approved_indications: Of the alternative agents discussed for maintaining fertility, only hCG is described as FDA-approved for use in males.
therapies_index.administration: May be used alone or with the other listed alternative agents in men with testosterone deficiency who want to maintain fertility.
monitoring: For patients using hCG, test testosterone no earlier than four weeks after treatment begins.

therapies_index.name: selective estrogen receptor modulators
therapies_index.mechanism: Described as promoting endogenous testosterone production.
therapies_index.administration: May be used alone or with the other listed alternative agents in men with testosterone deficiency who want to maintain fertility. Patients with low or low/normal LH are also described as candidates, particularly if they wish to preserve fertility.

therapies_index.name: anastrozole
monitoring: Test testosterone no earlier than four weeks after treatment begins.

therapies_index.name: clomiphene citrate
monitoring: Test testosterone no earlier than four weeks after treatment begins.

therapies_index.name: lifestyle modifications
therapies_index.administration: The guideline advises counseling all men with testosterone deficiency about strategies such as weight loss or maintaining weight within the recommended range and increasing physical activity. It advises counseling patients who are overweight or obese about weight-loss programs alongside testosterone therapy.

therapies_index.name: radical prostatectomy
therapies_index.administration: Discussed as prior treatment in men with prostate cancer who may subsequently be considered for testosterone therapy.
monitoring: The guideline discusses an undetectable postoperative PSA when considering subsequent testosterone therapy.

therapies_index.name: RT
therapies_index.administration: Discussed as prior treatment in men with prostate cancer; the guideline also identifies testicular radiation exposure as a reason to consider measuring testosterone.

therapies_index.name: androgen deprivation therapy
therapies_index.administration: Mentioned as a possible prior treatment among men with prostate cancer who received RT.
